source.title: Dynamic sparsity in tree-structured feed-forward layers at scale
source.authors: Reza Sedghi; Robin Schiewer; Anand Subramoney; David Kappel

record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out perplexity across feed-forward architecture variants, but does not test the original scaling-law measurements or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports language-model losses and perplexities, but does not sweep parameter count, training tokens, or compute to test a power law or extrapolation. It uses a 20:1 training-token-to-parameter ratio following Hoffmann et al. without testing that allocation rule. The relevant results for V4 are the parameter-scale-matched architecture comparisons in Tables 1 and 6. Downstream benchmark scores, training-loss curves, and the cited pretrained-model results do not test any other version.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks its own sparse tree-structured feed-forward (FFF) layer against dense FF and MoE baselines. It adopts the Hoffmann et al. 20:1 token-to-parameter ratio as a training recipe and does not test it. No power-law fit, size sweep, extrapolation or allocation test is reported. V4 concerns how dense-transformer shape (depth, width, aspect ratio) affects loss at fixed parameter count. Swapping dense FF blocks for hard-routed sparse trees or MoE changes the computation type and active compute, not shape. FFF tree depth is a hyperparameter of the study's own layer, not transformer depth. So the perplexity comparisons are the study's method against baselines, not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors claim FFF layers, activating under 5% of FF units, match dense baselines at 1.3B scale (perplexity typically within 10%). They also identify an emergent auto-pruning effect from hard routing plus GELU, and show that post-GELU placement balances tree use.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates sparse tree-structured feed-forward layers rather than fitting the original scaling-law relationships. It adopts a 20:1 token-to-parameter ratio following Hoffmann et al. but does not test that rule.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity varies with tree depth, nonlinearity placement, dataset, and training regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing dense FF blocks with hard-routed sparse trees raises held-out perplexity at fixed total size. The rise is modest at shallow trees (125M: 23.78 dense vs 25.91 at d=3) and grows with tree depth/sparsity (29.37 at d=7); MoE shows a similar trend with expert count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed model size and token budget, conditional-sparsity FF layers cost held-out loss that grows with sparsity level.

record.problems: The architecture comparisons are limited to particular FFF, FFFpost, and MoE variants. The 1.3B fine-tuning perplexities lack a dense baseline for the same fine-tuning regime; several larger-model scaling results are training-loss plots rather than held-out-loss measurements.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant held-out perplexity values from Tables 1 or 6 were omitted. The 300B-token pretrained reference and results in downstream-task tables were excluded because they do not test the versions beyond the architecture comparisons recorded here.

untested.parts: 20:1 tokens-per-parameter ratio adopted from Hoffmann et al. as a recipe; not varied or tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels rest on an arbitrary 10% threshold and on treating sparse-FF type as 'shape'; I removed them. The 2.7B/6.7B results are training-loss curves only. FFF parameter matching to dense is not explicitly stated.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or held-out-loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction from smaller runs is compared with larger runs.
The study adopts a 20:1 token-to-parameter ratio following Hoffmann et al.; it does not vary compute or test how the optimal parameter and token counts grow.
The comparisons vary tree depth, sparsity, and nonlinearity placement; they do not broadly vary dense-transformer depth, width, or other standard architecture dimensions.
The vision experiment evaluates FFF performance, not whether a power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.
Downstream scores are reported, but the study does not test whether they are predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across setups or fitting choices.

relation.reason: The study uses the scaling-law training recipe and reports its own method's performance. Its model-size comparisons assess sparse-layer scalability rather than any listed scaling-law version.

tranche.reason: Section 6.1 adopts Hoffmann et al.'s approximately 20:1 token-to-parameter training recipe. Results benchmark sparse-layer replacements without testing power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or systematic shape invariance.

source_check.notes: All 20 numerical rows match the source, but they are own-method comparisons rather than scaling-law evidence. The rationale needs two qualifications: Appendix C includes 2.7B and 6.7B size comparisons, and Section 6.2 itself describes perplexity differences as typically within 10%.
